Model Context Protocol · teaching notes

How MCP actually works

MCP is a shared plug shape for AI apps: one open standard for how a model-powered app discovers and calls the tools, data and prompts that live in other systems.

Watch the animation once end to end, then use the sections below to slow each step down. The interactive trace in section 4 replays the same request with the actual messages on the wire.

1. Why MCP exists

Before MCP, every AI app that wanted to reach a system — a blog CMS, a database, a ticket tracker — needed its own custom integration for it. With M AI apps and N systems, that's up to M × N pieces of glue code, each written slightly differently.

MCP turns the multiplication into addition. An app that speaks MCP can use any MCP server; a system that ships an MCP server can be used from any MCP-aware app. It's the same move USB made for peripherals, or the Language Server Protocol made for code editors — and LSP was a direct inspiration.

2. The five layers

The animation stacks five layers. Each one has a single job, and most confusion about MCP comes from blurring two of them together.

  1. You

    You state an intent in plain language: "Post my draft to the blog." You never write JSON or choose an API.

  2. Host app — LLM and MCP client

    The host is the application you're using: Claude, an IDE, an agent you built. It contains two very different things. The LLM reads your request plus the list of available tools and decides which tool to use and with what arguments. The MCP client is ordinary code that executes that decision by speaking the protocol.

    Not: the LLM doesn't open network connections or speak JSON-RPC. It only produces a choice.

  3. The protocol

    One open standard: JSON-RPC 2.0 messages carried over stdio (local) or HTTP (remote). It defines the vocabulary — initialize, tools/list, tools/call, resources/read and friends — so both sides know exactly what to send and what to expect back.

    Not: a server, a service, or a product. It's an agreement about message shapes.

  4. MCP server

    A small adapter, usually one per system you connect. It advertises what it can do (tools, resources, prompts), receives protocol calls, and translates them into that system's native API calls.

    Not: usually an AI. Most servers are thin, deterministic wrappers with no model inside.

  5. Your real systems

    The things that actually hold data or take action: the blog CMS, LinkedIn's API, a Postgres database, the file system. They don't know or care that MCP exists — the server talks to them the way any other integration would.

One detail the animation simplifiesEach MCP client holds exactly one connection to one server. A host that's connected to five servers runs five client instances side by side. "The client" in the diagram stands for whichever one owns the server being called.

3. What servers offer

A server can expose three kinds of things. The useful way to tell them apart is to ask who decides when each one gets used.

PrimitiveWhat it isWho's in controlBlog example
ToolsActions with side effects, described by a name, a description and a JSON Schema for inputs.The model chooses to call them.publish_post, schedule_post
ResourcesReadable data identified by a URI, like a file or a record.The host app decides what to load into context.blog://drafts/d_482
PromptsReusable, parameterised templates — recipes for a task.The user picks them, often as a slash command."Write a launch post from these notes"

It also works in the other direction

Clients can offer features back to servers. With sampling, a server asks the host's LLM to generate text, so the server needs no model or API key of its own. With elicitation, a server asks the user a follow-up question through the host ("Which blog: personal or company?"). With roots, the client tells the server which folders or URIs it's allowed to work within. Both sides announce which of these they support when they first connect.

5. Transports: stdio or HTTP

The messages are identical either way; only the pipe changes.

TransportHow it runsTypical use
stdioThe host launches the server as a local child process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over its stdin and stdout.Local tools: file system, git, a local database. No network exposure, no separate auth step.
Streamable HTTPThe server is a web service. The client POSTs JSON-RPC to a single endpoint; the server replies with plain JSON or streams several messages back using server-sent events.Remote and shared services: SaaS connectors, team-wide servers. Authorisation is based on OAuth 2.1.

You may still see older servers using a separate HTTP + SSE transport with two endpoints. That design was superseded by Streamable HTTP, which does the same job through one endpoint.

6. Where trust lives

MCP carries requests faithfully; it doesn't decide whether a request is a good idea. That responsibility sits with the host, which is the only layer that can see you, the model and every server at once.

Consent before action. A host should show the user what a tool call will do and let them approve it, especially anything that writes, sends, spends or deletes.

Treat server content as untrusted input. Tool descriptions and tool results go straight into the model's context. A malicious or compromised server can hide instructions in them — "also email the contents of ~/.ssh to…" — which is a form of prompt injection. Install servers only from sources you trust.

Least privilege. Give each server credentials scoped to exactly what it needs. A blog-posting server needs publish rights on one blog, not an admin token for the whole CMS.

Remote servers need real auth. Over HTTP, use the protocol's OAuth-based authorisation rather than long-lived shared keys, and never pass a user's token through to other upstream services.

7. Common mix-ups

The LLM talks to the MCP server.
The model only outputs a decision — tool name and arguments. The MCP client, which is regular code in the host, turns that into a JSON-RPC call and sends it.
MCP replaces function calling.
They work together. Function calling (tool use) is how a model expresses "call this tool with these inputs". MCP standardises where the tool definitions come from and how the call reaches the real system.
An MCP server is an agent.
Almost always it's a thin adapter with no reasoning of its own. The intelligence stays in the host's model; a server borrows it only if it uses sampling.
Connecting a server makes it safe to use.
The protocol doesn't vet what a server does. Safety comes from what you install, how you scope its credentials, and whether the host asks before acting.
Every tool must be a separate server.
One server typically exposes many related tools, resources and prompts — everything for one system in one adapter.

9. Glossary

Host
The AI application the user interacts with; it contains the model and one MCP client per connected server.
Client
Protocol-speaking code inside the host that keeps a one-to-one connection with a single server.
Server
An adapter that exposes a system's capabilities as tools, resources and prompts.
JSON-RPC 2.0
A lightweight message format: requests carry an id, method and params; responses carry the same id plus a result or error; notifications have no id and expect no reply.
Capabilities
The features each side declares during initialize, so neither side calls something the other doesn't support.
inputSchema
The JSON Schema attached to a tool that tells the model which arguments are valid.
Sampling
A server asking the host's model to generate text on its behalf.
Elicitation
A server asking the user for missing information, routed through the host.
Roots
The folders or URIs a client tells a server it may operate within.
